Emma shares both sets of John’s grandparents, so they are first cousins through both parental lines – i.e., double first cousins.

W is the sister of P's mother, making W P's maternal aunt. W's child M is therefore P's first cousin. P's son Q is one generation below P. The child of one's first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Hence M is Q's first cousin once removed.

P's mother’s brother U is P’s maternal uncle. U’s daughter C is therefore the child of P’s maternal uncle, making C P’s first cousin on the mother’s side. The marriage to D (who is the son of P’s paternal aunt) does not affect the blood relationship. Hence, C is a first cousin of P.

Adam and Brian are full brothers, so their children Carl and Diana are first cousins. Ethan is Diana's son, placing him one generation below Diana. The relationship between a person and the child of their first cousin is defined as first cousins once removed. No half‑sibling or adoption conditions apply, so the correct choice is A.

M's father's sister is M's paternal aunt; her child L is M's first cousin on the father's side. M's mother's brother is M's maternal uncle; his child N is M's first cousin on the mother's side. The aunt and uncle come from two unrelated parental lines, so L and N's parents are not blood‑related. Consequently L and N share no common ancestor, making them unrelated by blood. They are not half‑first cousins, as that would require their parents to be half‑siblings. Therefore the most precise term is that they have no blood relation.

R's maternal uncle's child is a first cousin on the mother's side; R's paternal aunt's child is a first cousin on the father's side. If both cousins are the same individual, that person is simultaneously a first cousin through both parents, which is defined as a double first cousin.

Emma is the child of Lily, who is John’s daughter, making Emma John’s granddaughter. She is also the child of Mary’s son, John’s nephew, which makes Emma John’s grandniece. English kinship terminology has no single word that simultaneously denotes both relations, so the correct choice is that she is both granddaughter and grandniece.

M and N share the same parents, and X and Y share another set of parents. A is the child of M (one of the first siblings) and X (one of the second siblings); B is the child of N (the other sibling from the first pair) and Y (the other sibling from the second pair). Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents—those of M/N and those of X/Y. Sharing two distinct lines of first‑cousin relationship makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Emma's mother and Tom are siblings, making Tom Emma's maternal uncle. Tom's daughter Lily is therefore Emma's first cousin. Lily's son Noah is one generation below Lily, so he is one generation below Emma's cousin. The relation between a person and the child of their cousin is "first cousin once removed".

M and N are siblings, so their children would be first cousins through that side. O and P are also siblings, making X and Y first cousins through the other side as well. Because X and Y share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of O/P), they are first cousins twice over, i.e., double first cousins. This is more precise than simply first cousins and does not fit the definitions of second or half‑first cousins.

M and S are siblings; W and N are siblings. M marries W, producing A. S marries N, producing B. A’s father (M) is the sibling of B’s father (S), and A’s mother (W) is the sibling of B’s mother (N). Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through two distinct sibling links—i.e., double first cousins, the most specific description.

R's maternal aunt (his mother's sister) is S's mother, making S a first cousin through the maternal line. R's paternal uncle (his father's brother) is S's father, making S a first cousin through the paternal line as well. Because S is related to R as a first cousin on both sides, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of a double first cousin.

Z’s father’s sister A is Z’s paternal aunt; her son B is Z’s paternal first cousin. Z’s mother’s brother C is Z’s maternal uncle; his daughter D is Z’s maternal first cousin. Both B and D are first cousins of Z, regardless of their marriage to each other. Hence the precise kinship term for D (or B) relative to Z is “first cousin.”

Adam and Ben share the same parents, making them full brothers. Clara and Dana share the same parents, making them full sisters. Their children X and Y each have a father who is a brother of the other's father and a mother who is a sister of the other's mother. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, which defines double first cousins.

A’s mother and B’s father are siblings, sharing a pair of grandparents. A’s father and B’s mother are also siblings, sharing a second pair of grandparents. Thus A and B share both sets of grandparents (each has the same maternal and paternal grandparents), which is the definition of double first cousins.
M is mother of N, O, and S (since S is N's sister). S is mother of R, making M R's grandmother. Therefore R is M's grandchild.

Anna's mother and Beth's father are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. Anna's father and Beth's mother are also siblings, providing a second set of shared grandparents. Thus Anna and Beth are each the child of two sibling pairs, meaning they share both grandparents. This defines double first cousins, the most precise term among the options.

Z and W are siblings. Their children Y and V are therefore first cousins. X is Y's child and U is V's child, making X and U the children of first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins, as they share the same great‑grandparents. Hence the kinship term is second cousins.

Ethan's father Adam and Felix's father Ben are brothers, making Ethan and Felix paternal first cousins. Ethan's mother Clara and Felix's mother Diana are sisters, making them maternal first cousins as well. When two individuals share both sets of grandparents because each of their parents are siblings, they are double first cousins. Thus the most precise term is double first cousins.

A and B share one parent, making them half‑siblings. The children of siblings are first cousins. When the siblings are half‑siblings, their children are first cousins who share only one grandparent, commonly called half‑first cousins. Thus C and D are half‑first cousins.

John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing a mother. That mother is a grandparent of both Alice (through John) and Bob (through Mary). Since Alice and Bob share only one grandparent, they are half‑first cousins, not full first cousins. No other marriages affect the lineage, so the relationship is determinable.

M and N are children of two brothers (P and R) and two sisters (Q and S). Therefore they share both paternal grandparents (parents of P and R) and maternal grandparents (parents of Q and S). This makes them first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins, the most precise standard term.

M and N are siblings, sharing a set of grandparents. X and Y are another pair of siblings, sharing a different set of grandparents. A’s parents are M (child of the first set) and X (child of the second set); B’s parents are N (child of the first set) and Y (child of the second set). Thus A and B each inherit both grandparent sets from the opposite side, meaning they are first cousins through both parental lines—i.e., double first cousins.

M and N are siblings, so A (M's daughter) and B (N's son) are first cousins. A marries B and their child is C. A's mother (M's wife) has a brother D, making D A's maternal uncle. D's daughter E is therefore A's first cousin. The generational gap between A (cousin) and C (A's child) is one, so E is one generation above C. The standard term for a first cousin of a parent is "first cousin once removed". Hence E and C are first cousins once removed.

John and Kate are siblings; Mary and Paul are siblings. Alex is child of John (brother) and Mary (sister). Bella is child of Kate (sister) and Paul (brother). Alex’s paternal grandparents are the parents of John and Kate, who are also Bella’s maternal grandparents. Alex’s maternal grandparents are the parents of Mary and Paul, who are also Bella’s paternal grandparents. Thus Alex and Bella share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

A is P's paternal aunt (father's sister) and B is P's maternal uncle (mother's brother). Their child C is the offspring of P's aunt and uncle from opposite sides of the family. Therefore C is P's first cousin through his father and also first cousin through his mother, making them double first cousins. No half relationship applies because they share both sets of grandparents. The precise term is double first cousin.

John's sister Mary is Lily's grandmother (Mary → son Peter → daughter Lily). A sibling's grandchild is a grandniece or grandnephew. The same Lily is also David's granddaughter, confirming the same relation. Therefore Lily is John's grandniece.

A's mother's brother is A's maternal uncle; his son is A's maternal first cousin. A's father's sister is A's paternal aunt; her daughter is A's paternal first cousin. The woman in question is that daughter, i.e., A's paternal first cousin. Thus her blood relation to A is that of a first cousin.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only one parent. Their children A and B each have that shared parent as a grandparent, but they do not share the other grandparent. Hence A and B share exactly one grandparent, making them half‑first cousins, the precise term among the options.

X is N's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and Y is N's paternal aunt (father's sister). X and Y, who are unrelated by blood, marry and have child Z. Z is therefore N's child of his maternal uncle (first‑cousin relationship) and also the child of his paternal aunt (another first‑cousin relationship). Being first cousins through both parental lines makes Z a double first cousin of N.

Alex and Ben are full brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Dana are full sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Thus P and Q share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most precise term.

R's mother's only brother is R's maternal uncle; his child X is the child of that uncle, making X R's first cousin. Similarly, R's father's only brother is R's paternal uncle; his child Y is also a first cousin of R. Whether S is X or Y, S is a child of an uncle of R, which is the definition of a first cousin. Thus the relationship is determinable as a first cousin.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle; M’s father’s sister is M’s paternal aunt. Their child N is the offspring of M’s maternal uncle, making N a first cousin on the mother’s side, and also the offspring of M’s paternal aunt, making N a first cousin on the father’s side. Thus N shares both sets of grandparents with M, which defines a double first‑cousin relationship.

P's father's sister is P's paternal aunt; P's mother's brother is P's maternal uncle. They marry each other, so their child M is simultaneously the child of P's paternal aunt and the child of P's maternal uncle. Thus M is P's first cousin on the father's side and also a first cousin on the mother's side, making M a double first cousin of P.

N's father (F) has a mother. Her sister is F's maternal aunt. M is the child of that sister, making M a first cousin of F. Since M is one generation above N (cousin of N's parent), M is N's first cousin once removed.

Y’s mother is X’s mother’s sister, making Y the child of X’s maternal aunt. Therefore Y is X’s first cousin by blood. Y is also married to X’s paternal aunt, giving him an uncle‑by‑marriage role, but the most precise direct kinship term is the blood relation first cousin.

P and Q are siblings, so Q is T's father. S, married to Q, is T's mother. R is S's sister, making R T's maternal aunt by blood. Additionally, R is married to P, Q's sibling, which also makes her an aunt by marriage, but the direct kinship term is aunt.

X's father M and Y's father N are siblings, making X and Y first cousins. Simultaneously, X's mother O and Y's mother P are siblings, creating another first‑cousin link. Because they are first cousins through both parental lines, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

L's mother and father each have exactly one brother. The son of L's maternal uncle (P) and the son of L's paternal uncle (Q) are each children of L's parents' siblings, which by definition are first cousins to L. Selecting either P or Q as S yields the same relation: first cousin.

X is the child of Y's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and also the child of Y's paternal aunt (father's sister). In each case X is Y's first cousin, and because both parental lines connect, X is a double first cousin. The standard term for that relationship is still "first cousin".

R's maternal uncle M's child C₁ is R's first cousin (maternal side). R's paternal uncle P's child C₂ is R's first cousin (paternal side). C₁ and C₂ are unrelated to each other, so their child S is the offspring of two of R's first cousins. In kinship terms, the child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. Since both parental lines give the same degree, S is R's first cousin once removed, not a double second cousin or any other term.
John's daughter Emma marries Alex, and they have a son Sam. Sam is therefore the child of John’s daughter, making Sam John’s grandson. No other direct kinship term fits this relationship.

John's daughter Lisa is Sam's mother, making Sam the child of John's child, i.e., his grandchild. The appropriate kinship term is grandson (assuming Sam is male). Therefore the correct choice is Grandson.

Anna and Ben share only their mother, making them half‑siblings. Their children Carl and Dana are therefore half‑first cousins (they share one grandparent). The children of half‑first cousins are half‑second cousins, sharing a single great‑grandparent. Eva (Carl’s child) and Frank (Dana’s child) thus fit this definition.

A's mother is B's aunt, so A is the child of B's aunt, making A and B first cousins. B is married to C, so the only link between A and C is through B's marriage. Standard English kinship terms for in‑laws cover only spouse, spouse's parents/siblings, siblings' spouses, and children's spouses. There is no accepted term for the relationship between a person's cousin and that cousin's spouse. Hence the connection is purely an affinal chain with no direct standard term, matching choice C.

N's father has an only sister (paternal aunt). Her child is M, making M N's first cousin on the father's side. N's mother has an only brother (maternal uncle). His child is also M, making M N's first cousin on the mother's side. Since M is the child of both the paternal aunt and the maternal uncle, the two sibling pairs (father–paternal aunt and mother–maternal uncle) have intermarried, producing a child who is a first cousin through both parental lines. This is the definition of a double first cousin.

Alex’s mother’s brother is Alex’s maternal uncle; Alex’s father’s sister is Alex’s paternal aunt. They marry each other and have Sam. Sam is therefore the child of Alex’s maternal uncle (making Sam a first cousin on the mother’s side) and also the child of Alex’s paternal aunt (making Sam a first cousin on the father’s side). Being a first cousin through both parental lines makes Sam a double first cousin of Alex.

S1 and S2 are full sisters, so their children share maternal grandparents. A and B are full brothers, so their children share paternal grandparents. D1 and D2 therefore share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins on both sides—i.e., double first cousins.

R's mother has one brother, making that brother R's maternal uncle. The uncle's child (X) is the child of a sibling of R's mother, which is the definition of a first cousin. Similarly, R's father has one sister, the paternal aunt, whose child (Y) is also the child of a sibling of R's father, also a first cousin. Whether S refers to X or Y, S is a child of a sibling of one of R's parents, thus S is R's first cousin.

M's mother and N's father are siblings, so they share the same parents. Therefore M (child of the mother) and N (child of the father) are each a child of a sibling, making them first cousins. The fact that M is married to N's sister does not affect blood relation. Hence the precise blood relation is first cousin.

Q's mother (M) has a mother (G). G's sibling (G_sib) is the aunt/uncle of M. The child of that sibling is L. Therefore L and M are first cousins (children of siblings). Since Q is the child of M, L is one generation above Q and is the cousin of Q's parent, which is the definition of a first cousin once removed.

X's mother is the sister of Y's father, and X's father is the brother of Y's mother. Thus each of X's parents is a sibling of one of Y's parents. Consequently X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

R is the son of O, who is N's sibling, making R N's nephew. Q is married to R, so Q is the spouse of N's nephew. Standard kinship terms allowed for in‑law relations do not cover a spouse of a nephew (they cover spouse, spouse's parents/siblings, siblings' spouses, children's spouses). Therefore Q has no standard direct relation to N, only an affinal chain.

Mary and Linda are full sisters, making them siblings. Their respective children, John (Mary's son) and Emma (Linda's daughter), are the children of two siblings. In standard kinship terminology, children of siblings are first cousins.

Lisa and Maya share only their mother, making them half‑sisters. Their children, Kevin and Nina, each inherit that common grandmother as a grandparent, but have different grandfathers. Thus Kevin and Nina share exactly one grandparent, not a full pair. In kinship terminology, children of half‑siblings are called half‑first cousins, distinguishing them from full first cousins who share both grandparents.

S_f, the only sibling of N’s father, is N’s paternal aunt/uncle; S_m, the only sibling of N’s mother, is N’s maternal aunt/uncle. They are married, and M is their child. Therefore M is N’s first cousin through the father’s side and also a first cousin through the mother’s side, making M a double first cousin of N.

M's mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle, making his child M’s first cousin on the maternal side. The same man is married to M’s father’s sister, who is M’s paternal aunt, so their child is also M’s first cousin on the paternal side. Because Y is a first cousin through both parents, they are double first cousins.

R's mother’s brother and R's father’s brother are each a sibling of one of R’s parents. The child of any sibling of a parent is, by definition, a first cousin of R. This relationship is the same regardless of whether the uncle is maternal or paternal, and it does not depend on the child’s gender. Hence the precise kinship term is "first cousin".

Q and U share a mother, making U a half‑sister of Q. Therefore U is M's half‑aunt. T, as U's spouse, is the husband of M's half‑aunt, which in everyday English is called an uncle (uncle‑by‑marriage). The standard kinship term is simply “uncle.”

Emily's mother is sister of Sarah's father, making Emily and Sarah first cousins. Sarah's son Daniel is one generation below Sarah, so Emily is Sarah's first cousin once removed to Daniel. Daniel's daughter Lily is another generation down, placing Lily two generations below Emily's cousin level. Therefore Emily is Lily's first cousin twice removed.

X and Y are brothers, so they share the same parents. A and B are sisters, sharing their own parents. C is the child of X and A; D is the child of Y and B. Therefore C and D are related through both paternal and maternal lines, each being first cousins on both sides. This dual connection makes them double first cousins, not half or second cousins.

A's mother’s brother B is A’s maternal uncle; B’s daughter C is A’s maternal first cousin. A's father’s sister D is A’s paternal aunt; D’s son E is A’s paternal first cousin. Thus both C and E are first cousins of A. Their child F is the offspring of A’s first cousin, which by kinship rules is a first cousin once removed (one generation down from the cousin). Hence the precise relation of F to A is first cousin once removed.

Mary's brother Tom is John’s maternal uncle; Peter's sister Linda is John’s paternal aunt. Tom and Linda’s daughter Emma is therefore the child of John’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Emma is thus John’s first cousin on his mother’s side and also his first cousin on his father’s side, sharing both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins.

N's father's only sister is N's paternal aunt. N's mother's only brother is N's maternal uncle. These two siblings are married and have child M. M is therefore the child of N's paternal aunt (making M a first cousin on the father's side) and also the child of N's maternal uncle (making M a first cousin on the mother's side). Being first cousins through both parental lines makes M a double first cousin of N.

M and N are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents (G1). O and P are siblings, sharing another set (G2). X’s parents are M (child of G1) and O (child of G2); Y’s parents are N (child of G1) and P (child of G2). Consequently X and Y inherit the same two grandparents from both parental lines. They are first cousins through M‑N and also first cousins through O‑P, making them double first cousins, the most precise term.

M and N share both parents, as do X and Y. A’s parents are M (child of grandparents P1,P2) and X (child of Q1,Q2). B’s parents are N (also child of P1,P2) and Y (also child of Q1,Q2). Therefore A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines. This is the definition of double first cousins.

P's mother is sibling of Q's father, and P's father is sibling of Q's mother. Thus each parent of P is a sibling of the opposite parent of Q. This matches the definition of double first cousins—children of two sibling pairs who intermarry. No other relations are implied.

M and N are siblings, so they share the same parents (paternal grandparents for X and Y). O and P are siblings, sharing another set of parents (maternal grandparents for X and Y). X’s parents are M (from the first sibling pair) and O (from the second pair); Y’s parents are N (the sibling of M) and P (the sibling of O). Thus X and Y share *both* sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins.

M is the child of J's paternal aunt (father's sister) making M a first cousin on the father's side, and also the child of J's maternal uncle (mother's brother) making M a first cousin on the mother's side. Being first cousins through both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, so M and N are first cousins through that parental pair. Likewise, M’s father is the brother of N’s mother, making them first cousins again through the other parental pair. With both parents of each being siblings, M and N share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins. Hence the most precise term is double first cousins.

Ethan's father Adam and Fiona's father Beth are siblings, giving them shared paternal grandparents. Ethan's mother Clara and Fiona's mother David are also siblings, giving them shared maternal grandparents. Thus Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two sibling pairs. The precise term for such a relationship is double first cousins.

Eva's father Paul and Omar's father Quentin are brothers, making Eva and Omar first cousins through their paternal line. Their mothers, Lisa and Maya, are sisters, making them first cousins through the maternal line as well. Because they are related as first cousins on both sides, they share both sets of grandparents, which is the definition of double first cousins.

Anna and Ben are siblings. Ben's daughter Clara is Anna's niece. Anna's son David is her direct offspring. Clara (niece) and David (son) have Ethan. Through David, Ethan is Anna's grandson. Through Clara, Ethan is the child of Anna's niece, which makes him a grandniece/nephew (often called great‑nephew). Thus Ethan holds both relations simultaneously.

M's father (P) and N's father (R) are brothers, making M and N first cousins on their paternal side. Similarly, M's mother (Q) and N's mother (S) are sisters, making them first cousins on their maternal side as well. Because they are first cousins through both parents, they are double first cousins. This is more specific than simply 'first cousins' and not a half relationship.

John and Peter are brothers; Mary and Anna are sisters. Lily is the child of John (brother of Peter) and Mary (sister of Anna). Sarah is the child of Peter (brother of John) and Anna (sister of Mary). Thus Lily and Sarah are children of two pairs of siblings, making them double first cousins. They share both sets of grandparents, but the kinship term remains first cousins.

X is R's maternal uncle, making his son Y R's maternal first cousin. Z is R's paternal aunt, making her daughter W R's paternal first cousin. The marriage between Y and W does not alter Y's blood relationship to R; Y remains R's first cousin. No half‑relation or in‑law term applies.

Adam and Brian are brothers, so their children share the same paternal grandparents. Clara and Diana are sisters, so their children share the same maternal grandparents. Therefore X and Y have both sets of grandparents in common, making them children of two sibling pairs. This relationship is defined as double first cousins, which is more specific than ordinary first cousins.

A and B are siblings, C and D are siblings, and each sibling pair marries the other pair. Therefore E (child of A and C) and F (child of B and D) share both sets of grandparents (the parents of A/B and the parents of C/D). Sharing both grandparent sets makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

Z’s father’s brother is the paternal uncle. He is married to Z’s mother’s sister, who is the maternal aunt. Therefore Z’s mother’s sister’s husband is the same individual as Z’s father’s brother, i.e., Z’s paternal uncle.

X’s mother and U are siblings, so U is X’s maternal uncle. U’s daughter Y is therefore X’s first cousin. Y’s son Z is the child of X’s cousin, which makes Z a first cousin once removed (the 'once removed' indicates a generational difference). This matches a standard kinship term.

The two brothers are siblings and the two sisters are siblings. Their children X and Y are each the product of a brother–sister pair, so X and Y share both sets of grandparents (paternal and maternal). Hence X and Y are double first cousins. The next generation, P (child of X) and Q (child of Y), are therefore the children of double first cousins. Children of first cousins are second cousins; children of double first cousins are double second cousins. Thus the most precise term is double second cousins.

N’s mother has one sibling (a maternal aunt/uncle) and N’s father has one sibling (a paternal aunt/uncle). M is the child of both of these siblings, meaning the maternal aunt/uncle and the paternal aunt/uncle have a child together. This situation occurs when two sets of siblings intermarry, producing a double first cousin relationship. A half‑first cousin would require only one shared grandparent, which is not the case. The relationship is determinable, so the correct choice is double first cousin.

Y's father's only sister is Y's paternal aunt; her child is Y's first cousin on the father's side. Y's mother's only brother is Y's maternal uncle; his child is Y's first cousin on the mother's side. X is the child of both the aunt and the uncle, meaning the aunt and uncle are married. Hence X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X a double first cousin of Y.

John's mother Mary and Laura are sisters, so Laura is John's maternal aunt. John’s father Peter and Thomas are brothers, so Thomas is John's paternal uncle. Emma is the daughter of Laura (maternal aunt) and Thomas (paternal uncle). Therefore Emma is John's first cousin through his mother and also his first cousin through his father, meaning they share both sets of grandparents. This makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

B is A's parent. B's sister C is A's aunt, and C's brother F is also B's sibling, making F another aunt/uncle of A. G is the child of F, so G is the child of A's aunt/uncle, which by standard kinship terms is a first cousin of A. Therefore the correct relation is first cousin.

Alice’s mother and Ben’s father are siblings, meaning they share both parents. Alice is the child of one sibling, Ben is the child of the other. Children of siblings are first cousins. No half‑sibling relationship exists, so the precise term is first cousins.

M and N are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. That mother is a grandparent to both X (M's daughter) and Y (N's son). Since X and Y have exactly one common grandparent, they are the children of half‑siblings, which defines the relationship of half‑first cousins.

John and Peter are brothers, so they share the same paternal grandparents. Mary and Susan are sisters, sharing the same maternal grandparents. Alice’s parents are John (paternal side) and Mary (maternal side); Bob’s parents are Peter (same paternal side as John) and Susan (same maternal side as Mary). Thus Alice and Bob share both sets of grandparents, making them the children of two sibling pairs. This is the definition of double first cousins.

N's father's only sister is N's paternal aunt; her child is N's cousin. N's mother's only brother is N's maternal uncle; his child is also N's cousin. Since M is the child of both the aunt and the uncle, those two are M's parents, making M a double first cousin of N. Thus the relation is first cousin.

P is the child of M's brother (B) and N's sister (S). Q is the child of M and N. Thus P and Q share M's parents as grandparents through B-M, and also share N's parents as grandparents through S-N. Sharing both paternal and maternal grandparent sets makes them double first cousins, the most precise term.

N's paternal aunt (father's sister) and N's maternal uncle (mother's brother) are married. Their child M is the offspring of N's father's sibling, making M a first cousin on the paternal side, and also the offspring of N's mother's sibling, making M a first cousin on the maternal side. Being a first cousin through both parental lines defines a double first cousin.

John and Paul are brothers, so Paul is Anna's paternal uncle. Mary's sister Lucy is Anna's maternal aunt. Ben is the child of Paul and Lucy, making him the child of both Anna's paternal uncle and maternal aunt. Thus Ben is the child of a sibling of each of Anna's parents, which is the definition of a first cousin (specifically a double first cousin, but still classified as a first cousin). No half‑cousin or in‑law term applies.

M is the parent of both D and B, making D and B siblings. Their respective children G (child of D) and W (child of B) are therefore the children of siblings, which by standard English kinship terminology are first cousins.

M and N are full siblings, so they share the same parents. P and Q are also full siblings, sharing another set of parents. A is the child of M and P; B is the child of N and Q. Thus A and B are each the child of one sibling from each parental pair, giving them both sets of grandparents in common. This makes them first cousins through both the maternal and paternal lines, i.e., double first cousins.

M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so they share one set of grandparents. Likewise, M’s father and N’s mother are siblings, giving a second shared set of grandparents. Thus M and N are children of two distinct sibling pairs, meaning they share both paternal and maternal grandparents. This relationship is defined as double first cousins.

L's mother has one brother, making him L's maternal uncle; his single child is L's maternal first cousin. L's father has one brother, the paternal uncle; his single child is L's paternal first cousin. Regardless of which brother's child is chosen as Z, Z is a first cousin of L. Hence the relationship is uniquely a first cousin.

L’s father’s sister is L’s paternal aunt; L’s mother’s brother is L’s maternal uncle.
